title: Thread pool, Task Parallel Library (TPL), and PLINQ
hook: The thread pool reuses operating system threads so you do not pay the cost of creating one per work item. The Task Parallel Library (TPL) schedules CPU-bound work on that pool; Parallel LINQ (PLINQ) splits sequence operations across cores.

blocks.text: ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem and Task.Run queue delegates to a shared pool of worker threads. Task represents asynchronous work — often I/O via async/await (module 13) or CPU work via Task.Run. Parallel.For and PLINQ (.AsParallel()) partition data across threads for CPU-bound algorithms. The pool grows under load and shrinks when idle.

entries.plainDefinition: A managed pool of worker threads shared by the runtime and your code.
entries.example: Task.Run schedules work on a pool thread.

entries.plainDefinition: APIs built around Task for parallel and asynchronous programming.
entries.example: Task.WhenAll, Parallel.ForEach, and PLINQ are TPL features.

entries.plainDefinition: Parallel execution of LINQ to Objects queries via .AsParallel().

blocks.text: Blocking the pool with synchronous I/O starves other work — that is why module 13 uses async for Redis and HTTP. CPU-bound CSV parsing or image resizing belongs on the pool via Task.Run or Parallel, not on the request thread. Misusing PLINQ on tiny collections adds overhead without speedup.

blocks.title: CPU vs I/O split
blocks.body: async/await for I/O waits. Task.Run or Parallel for CPU-bound work that would block a thread for milliseconds of computation.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Identify CPU-bound section
items.body: Hashing, compression, parsing millions of rows — not network waits.

items.title: Choose API
items.body: Task.Run for a chunk; Parallel.ForEach for data parallelism; PLINQ for LINQ-style queries.

items.title: Avoid oversubscription
items.body: Do not nest Parallel inside Parallel without throttling.

items.title: Return to caller
items.body: await Task.Run(...) keeps the API async-friendly for ASP.NET Core.

snippet.label: Task.Run for CPU-bound work
snippet.explanation: File read is I/O; hashing is CPU. Task.Run moves hashing off the request thread to a pool thread.

snippet.label: Parallel.ForEach for CSV rows
snippet.explanation: Partitions row parsing across up to four threads. Use ConcurrentBag for thread-safe collection.

snippet.label: PLINQ with degree limit
snippet.explanation: PLINQ parallelizes the Where filter. Only worth it for large sequences and non-trivial predicates.

blocks.title: Parallelism models
rows: No built-in PLINQ; manual chunking to workers

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Task.Run for trivial work — overhead exceeds benefit. PLINQ on ten items. Blocking .Result on pool threads causing starvation. Using Parallel when work is I/O-bound — use async instead.

interviewTakeaways: Thread pool reuses threads; Task.Run is for CPU-bound work off the caller thread.
async/await is for I/O; do not confuse with data parallelism.
PLINQ and Parallel need enough work to justify thread coordination cost.
commonPitfalls: Unbounded Parallel.ForEach on millions of tiny items.
Blocking waits that starve the pool.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node worker_threads are the JS analogue for CPU parallelism. The main thread event loop is closer to async I/O in C#.
